solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Determined to shag someone in connection with article (fashion)

parts.note: 'on' means about or concerning, as in a talk on art
the definite article
to fashion something is to make it

explanation.surface: Someone set on a sexual conquest, all in the name of some fashion article.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed '(fashion)' looks like a magazine section label, but it is a verb meaning to build or produce.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a person hunting for a sexual partner, or more generally pushing hard for personal gain.

clue.text: Begs, with future looking grim — it's a stratagem

indicators.note: something looking grim is in a bad state, so these letters are in poor shape and need rearranging

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone pleads desperately because their prospects look bleak, and the pleading is only a trick.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words are mixed together as one pool of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a deceitful trick or scheme used to achieve an aim or escape a difficulty.

clue.text: Choose one associated with Donald Trump's extremes, welcomed by redneck?

indicators.note: a guest welcomed by a host is taken in, so one part goes inside the other

parts.note: a hick is an unsophisticated country person, like a redneck

indicators.note: things associated with each other go together, so one part sits next to the other

parts.note: 'an' is the indefinite article, meaning one

indicators.note: extremes are the two far ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the name

explanation.surface: A question about whether a Trump supporter from the rural South gets to pick someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The redneck fits Trump's rural base in the surface, which hides that it is only a host word wrapping the other pieces. 'Associated with' just joins two pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To hand-pick is to select carefully and personally, so it works as a stronger synonym for choosing.

clue.text: Death process that is taken up by crooked gang

indicators.note: in a down clue, taking something up lifts it from bottom to top, so its letters run backwards
taken by a group means held within it, so one part sits inside the other
something crooked is bent out of shape, so the letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
i.e. is the Latin abbreviation id est, meaning that is

explanation.surface: A corrupt gang carries out some grim procedure ending in someone's death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Process' belongs with 'Death' as the definition, not an indicator. In a down clue, 'taken up' turns the abbreviation upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Growing old is the slow biological decline that leads, eventually, to the end of life, so it is the dying process.

clue.text: Wife with joint gets bellyache

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife
a hinge is a movable joint, on a door or in the body

explanation.surface: A wife who has smoked a joint ends up with a stomach ache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a cannabis cigarette or a cut of meat; it is the pivot a door swings on. 'Bellyache' is the verb, to complain, not a stomach pain.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal verbs for complaining persistently and peevishly; whinge is the British form.

clue.text: Band's jacket recommendation — black's out

indicators.note: something that is out is gone or excluded, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: a blurb is the promotional praise printed on a book jacket
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A rock group endorses a jacket, and the black one is sold out.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the final B from BLURB. The surface suggests a band's merchandise; the jacket is a book's dust jacket. Blur were a leading 1990s Britpop band.
explanation.definitionFit: Blur is the name of a famous English rock group fronted by Damon Albarn, so it is an example of a pop group.

clue.text: Duke possibly gets some knob-lengthening

indicators.note: getting some of something means taking only a portion of it, a run of letters inside the phrase

parts.note: the letters sit inside, straddling the hyphen

explanation.surface: An aristocrat signs up for some dubious penis-enlargement treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from the N of 'knob' into the start of 'lengthening'.
explanation.definitionFit: A duke is the highest rank of the peerage, so a duke is one example of an aristocrat; 'possibly' marks the example.

clue.text: A real pain, e.g. a urinal malfunction

indicators.note: a malfunction is something going wrong, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: the abbreviation for 'for example', letters taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A broken urinal is offered as an example of something really irritating.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbreviation's letters are used as they stand; the full stops vanish. 'A real pain' looks like slang for a nuisance, but it means a literal pain.
explanation.definitionFit: The medical term names an intense, sharp pain running along a nerve, so it is a genuine physical ache.

clue.text: In which 'X' often makes an appearance with large fancy pyjama bottom round knob end

definitions.text: In which 'X' often makes an appearance

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so one part wraps the other
a fancy version is an elaborate reworking, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of oversized fancy pyjamas wrapped round something rude, with a kiss X added.
explanation.walkthrough: LARGE becomes ALGER, then the A is added to make ALGERA, which goes round B. 'X' looks like a kiss or an adult rating; it is the classic unknown.
explanation.definitionFit: The branch of mathematics uses letters such as x to stand for unknown quantities in equations.

clue.text: This is a bit unusual for a predictable celeb mag

definitions.text: This is a bit unusual for a predictable celeb mag

parts.note: surface reading: something surprising has happened at a dull gossip magazine
setter's reading: the magazine's own title is the greeting people say when something takes them by surprise

explanation.surface: A sardonic remark that a formulaic celebrity magazine has, for once, done something surprising.
explanation.walkthrough: The greeting is also an exclamation of surprise ('Hello, what's this?'), so the remark about something unusual is exactly what the magazine's name says. Hello! is a British celebrity gossip weekly.
explanation.definitionFit: The British celebrity weekly carries the greeting as its title, and the same word expresses mild surprise.

clue.text: Giving head badly (tense inside), so despised

indicators.note: inside means within, so one letter goes into the middle of the others
doing something badly means doing it wrongly, so the letters come out in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as written
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Someone performed oral sex poorly while nervous, and was scorned for it.
explanation.walkthrough: HEAD is shuffled to HAED and T is put in the middle. 'Tense' looks like an adjective for nerves; it is the grammar term.
explanation.definitionFit: To despise someone is to feel strong contempt or loathing, so the past participles are synonyms.

clue.text: Current applied to enlarge bust, for the most part

indicators.note: applying one thing to another puts them together side by side

parts.note: 'in' means current or fashionable, as in the in thing

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the letters are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An electrical current is applied as a breast-enlargement treatment, mostly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' wants to be electricity (I in physics), but here it means fashionable. 'Bust' looks like the body part; it means broken.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means usually, as a rule, or in most cases, which is what for the most part says.

clue.text: (&14) An odious aspect of you, your partner might wake up to?

definitions.text: An odious aspect of you, your partner might wake up to?

parts.note: surface reading: an unpleasant side of your character

parts.words: your partner might wake up to
parts.note: setter's reading: 'odious' hints at odour, a smell your bedmate meets on waking

explanation.surface: A partner gradually realising, as people do, some unpleasant trait of yours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wake up to' sounds like coming to realise something; read literally, it is what greets them on waking beside you. 'Odious' nudges toward odour.
explanation.definitionFit: The stale smell on the breath after a night's sleep is exactly the unpleasant thing a bedmate notices on waking.

clue.text: see 13ac
Make light of one victory in Test, Cyclops only half despatched

indicators.note: in places one thing within another
only half means the rest is cut away, so just the front part is kept

parts.note: a test is a trial
the setter Cyclops refers to themself as I
to despatch something is to send it off
the Roman numeral for one
V for victory

explanation.surface: Downplaying a single win in a cricket Test match while the setter is only half beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Test' looks like cricket (a Test is an international match) but just means trial. Setters often call themselves I or ME, and Cyclops is this setter's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To make light of something is to treat it as unimportant, which is what reducing it to a trivial matter does.

clue.text: The scan's bad? Balls to be restrained

indicators.note: bad means faulty, so the letters are out of their proper order

parts.note: taken as written
Ed Balls is a former Labour cabinet minister turned TV presenter

explanation.surface: A patient gets a bad scan result and swears 'Balls!', a British expletive for nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' reads as an exclamation or as testicles, but it stands for the politician's first name. The 's is just 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone chastened has been subdued or humbled by a rebuke, so they are restrained in manner.

clue.text: Unshackled Nick, recklessly drinking wife's punch

indicators.note: drinking means taking in, so one letter goes inside the rest
acting recklessly means acting wildly, so the letters are thrown about

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A man called Nick, freed from restraint, guzzles his wife's fruit punch with abandon.
explanation.walkthrough: W is taken into the fourteen letters before they are rearranged. 'Punch' looks like the drink; it is a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is jokey slang for a blow to the mouth with the fist, a fist being served like food.

clue.text: Storm after barmy Net candidate

indicators.note: after means following, so one part comes behind the other
barmy is British slang for crazy, so the letters go haywire

parts.note: taken as written
to storm is to rage or rant

explanation.surface: An outburst follows a crazy candidate who is popular on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Storm' is a verb meaning to rage, not weather; 'after' puts it second, though it is printed first.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrant is someone who enters a competition or exam, which makes them a candidate for it.

clue.text: Have a lie-in here and you'll be late

definitions.text: Have a lie-in here and you'll be late

parts.note: surface reading: oversleeping in your bed
setter's reading: 'late' means deceased, as in the late Mr Smith

explanation.surface: A warning that staying in this bed too long will make you late for work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' is the obituary sense, dead, so the place you lie and become 'late' is where people die.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the bed where someone lies in their final hours, so lying there ends with them deceased.

clue.text: Let's give a wave before sex

indicators.note: before means in front of, so one part comes first

parts.note: to perm hair is to give it a permanent wave
'it' is a coy word for sex, as in doing it

explanation.surface: A cheery invitation to wave to each other before getting down to sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let's' splits as Let plus 's, short for is. 'Give a wave' is the hairdressing perm, not a hand gesture.
explanation.definitionFit: To let someone do something is to allow it, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Ex-PM at border riot?

indicators.note: at means next to, so one part is placed right beside the other

parts.note: Theresa May, British prime minister 2016 to 2019
a hem is the border of a piece of cloth

explanation.surface: A former prime minister turns up at a disturbance on the national border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Border' suggests a frontier; it is the edge of a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayhem is violent disorder and chaos, which is what a riot is; the clue uses the noun loosely.

clue.text: Union's bête noire, i.e. Sun — "it's a disease!"

parts.note: a scab is a strike-breaker, hated by trade unions
the abbreviation's letters taken as written
S is the abbreviation for Sunday or sun

explanation.surface: Trade unions' great enemy, namely the Sun newspaper, denounced as a disease.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a Murdoch tabloid long hostile to unions, which makes the surface plausible; here it is just S.
explanation.definitionFit: Scabies is a contagious, itchy skin condition caused by mites burrowing under the skin.

clue.text: Rex, into pop star, might get balled

definitions.note: the definition describes the answer rather than naming it

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so one letter is placed inside

parts.note: Sting is the singer, former frontman of the Police
R is the abbreviation for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A man named Rex, a fan of a pop star, hopes to get the singer into bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balled' is meant as rolled into a ball, not the vulgar sense the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Twine is commonly wound into a ball for storage, so it is a thing that might be rolled up that way.

clue.text: Temperature raised, showing some leg

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for temperature
something raised is high up

explanation.surface: A hemline goes up and the temperature in the room rises with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' reads as a verb for the temperature, but it is an adjective supplying the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper part of the leg between hip and knee is one portion of it, so it is some of a leg.

clue.text: The bride and groom's drunk, mate

parts.note: happy is informal for slightly tipsy
to mate animals is to pair them

explanation.surface: At a wedding someone remarks that the groom is drunk, calling a friend 'mate'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mate' reads as a matey form of address, but it is the verb meaning to couple.
explanation.definitionFit: Newlyweds are traditionally toasted as a joyful couple on their wedding day, so the phrase stands for them.

clue.text: Virgin gets up, up and on

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written
re means on or concerning, as in business letters

explanation.surface: A virgin finally rises out of bed and gets going.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'up' is the letters, the second tells you to turn them over.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, virgin means untouched or unspoilt, the same sense as clean and unsullied.

clue.text: Share bed, to get around Labour's leader

indicators.note: getting around something means encircling it, so one part wraps the other

parts.note: to bed someone is to have sex with them, informally to have them

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the party name

explanation.surface: A politician agrees to share a bed with someone in order to win over the Labour leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Share bed' looks like one phrase but splits: the definition is the first word, the wordplay starts with 'bed'.
explanation.definitionFit: To divide something into two equal portions is to split it with another person, one half each.

clue.text: Stuff Bush? Senate's finally lost

indicators.note: something lost has gone missing, so a letter is removed

parts.note: George Bush, father and son, both US presidents

indicators.note: finally means at the very end, so only the last letter counts

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Should Bush be stuffed now that his party has lost the Senate?
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the first E from GEORGE. 'Stuff' looks like a dismissive remark about Bush; it is the verb to eat greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: To stuff yourself is to overeat greedily, and gorge as a verb carries exactly that meaning.

clue.text: State of 'X', the FBI agent on drugs?

indicators.note: on means placed against or next to, so one part follows another

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten
Eliot Ness, the lawman who pursued Al Capone
E is slang for ecstasy, so two Es are drugs

explanation.surface: A question about the condition of Mr X, an FBI agent supposedly high on narcotics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' reads as condition; it is a US state. Ness was strictly a Prohibition Treasury agent, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennessee is one of the fifty American states, home of Nashville and Memphis, so it is an example.
